municated to the South African Republic on the 2nd August, but the Government of the Republic were extremely unwilling to accept the joint enquiry, and an alternative proposal for a five years' franchise was made in August by the State Attorney, Mr. Smuts, to Her Majesty's Agent, Mr. Greene, on three assumptions. These assumptions were (1) that Her Majesty's Government would not in future interfere in the internal affairs of the Republic; (2) that Her Majesty's Government would not insist further upon the assertion of suzerainty, the controversy being allowed tacitly to drop (this point had acquired special importance since the South African Republic, on the 9th of May, had claimed the status of a sovereign international state); (3) that arbitration without foreign element should be conceded.

The proposal was put forward in writing by the Republic in notes dated the 19th and 21st August, and the three "assumptions" were put forward as express conditions. To these notes Her Majesty's Government replied, on the 28th August, that they could not bind themselves never to intervene again, but they expressed the hope that further intervention would be unnecessary if the franchise was granted. As to suzerainty they referred to their despatch in which they had intimated their refusal to continue the discussion; and as to arbitration, they agreed to discuss the form of a tribunal. The South African Republic, thereupon, in notes of the 1st and 2nd September, withdrew their five years' offer, and officially declared their objections to the joint enquiry, which they represented was an interference with the independence of the country. Her Majesty's Government then (8th September), being convinced by accumulating evidence of the unworkable character of the law which had been passed, while maintaining their position as regards interference and suzerainty, declared that they would be satisfied with a franchise on the five years' basis if shown by an enquiry, either unilateral or joint, not to be encumbered with impossible conditions. If this was acceded to they were ready to have a conference about arbitration, &c., but, failing acceptance, they would have to formulate their own proposals for a final settlement. To this the Government of the Republic replied by maintaining their withdrawal of the five years franchise unless accepted with the conditions above stated, and called on Her Majesty's Government to revert to the proposal for a joint commission on the seven years' franchise. On the 22nd of September Her Majesty's Government repeated their views, and stated that their own proposals for a settlement would be formulated later.

After some correspondence between the President of the Orange Free State and the High Commissioner, in which the High Commissioner, as late as the 5th of October, said that any definite proposal would still be considered, the South African Republic, without waiting for Her Majesty's Government to formulate their proposals, handed to the British Agent an ultimatum, dated 9th October, requiring the instant withdrawal of British troops on the borders of the Republic, and the removal of all reinforcements which had arrived in South Africa since the 1st of June, and demanding an answer by five o'clock on the 11th of October. It was deemed impossible by Her Majesty's Government to discuss such a demand, and war broke out accordingly. The Orange Free State, in pursuance of a resolution passed on the 27th of September, threw in its lot with the Transvaal.

A great exodus from the Rand had begun some time before the actual outbreak of war, the Government of the Republic having been commandeering and making other preparations for war, and so much distress resulted from the crowding of thousands of homeless refugees into the British Colonies that relief funds were started in this country.

On the outbreak of war, the Boers immediately invaded British territory to the south-east and west of the Republics. The operations on the western side were chiefly concerned with the investment of Mafeking and Kimberley. On the 12th of October an armoured train was wrecked by the Boers at Kraai Pan, and 16 men with 2 guns were captured. On the 15th of October an attack on Mafeking was repulsed with loss, and the town was successfully held by Colonial and a few Imperial troops, under Col. Baden-Powell, with great gallantry and fertility of resource. Kimberley was held with equal success against a large force of Boers. Meantime the main body of the Boers invaded Natal under General Joubert. The British garrison, which had been reinforced from India, and received valuable assistance from the Colonial forces and levies largely raised from the refugees arriving from the Rand, was encamped at Ladysmith, with an advanced outpost at Dundee. The first considerable engagement of the war occurred at the latter place on the 20th of October, where General Symons attacked and repulsed a Boer commando under Lucas Meyer, himself falling mortally wounded. A detachment of hussars and mounted infantry sent in pursuit of the retreating Boers was captured. The arrival of larger forces of the enemy necessitated falling back on Ladysmith; and this movement was skilfully executed by General Yule, who had succeeded to the command. On the 21st of October the British army at Ladysmith attacked a Boer commando at Elandslaagte, and inflicted a severe defeat. On the 24th, with the view of safeguarding General Yule's retreat to Ladysmith, General White engaged and dispersed the enemy at Rietfontein. On the 26th General Yule arrived at Ladysmith, and four days later Sir G. White made a reconnoissance with the combined forces. During the engagement which then took place two battalions and a mountain battery were cut off and captured by the Boers. Ladysmith was shortly after surrounded by the Boers and communication cut. On the 3rd of November Colenso was evacuated, and the garrison there fell back on Estcourt.

Meanwhile troops were on the way from England. An Army Corps was organized on the 17th of October, six days after the outbreak of war, a portion of the reserves having previously been called out, Sir Redvers Buller, who had been selected for the chief command, left for the Cape, and from the 20th of October transports left daily with large bodies of troops, guns and stores. The Governments of Canada and of all the Australian Colonies offered the services of contingents, and the offer was gratefully accepted; the despatch of troops from the different colonies was rapidly organised, and they left amidst enthusiastic demonstrations of loyalty. Offers of troops were also made by several of the Crown Colonies, and by the Federated Malay States, but it was not found possible to accept them.

As the troops from England arrived, a move forward was made in two directions. A Natal relief column prepared for an advance to the relief of Ladysmith. On the 23rd of November General Hildyard, who was commanding the garrison at Estcourt, attacked the Boers interrupting his line of communication, and forced them to retire. Sir Redvers Buller left Capetown for
Natal to direct the general plan of advance, and by the end of November the British forces had arrived near Colenso. While preparations for the relief of Ladysmith were in progress several successful sorties were made by the invested troops, and guns were destroyed, the news being conveyed to the advancing column by searchlight and heliographic signals. On December 15th Sir R. Buller made an attack on the enemy and attempted to cross the Tugela, but he had to retire to his camp at Chieveley after suffering severely in casualties and abandoning a large number of guns. On the western side a force under Lord Methuen pushed up along the railway to the relief of Kimberley. On the 23rd of November he attacked the Boers at Belmont and dispersed them. Two days later he pushed aside a further force at Emslin, and on the 28th November he forced a large body of the enemy to evacuate a strong position at the Modder River. He was then delayed for some days whilst the bridge over the Modder was being reconstructed and reinforcements and stores sent up to him. Searchlight communication was meanwhile established with the garrison, who were active in taking aggressive measures wherever possible. On December 11th Lord Methuen attacked the enemy at Magersfontein, but was unsuccessful in carrying the position. After remaining on his ground till the following day, he fell back on the Modder River. The losses in the engagement were heavy.

The northern borders of Cape Colony, where there were few British garrisons, were invaded by parties of Orange Free State Boers, with the apparent object of gaining recruits from the Dutch residents in the Colony, in which they were partially successful. General Gatacre, on his arrival, took command of the British troops in these districts. His first important action took place on the 10th of December, when he was unsuccessful in a night attack on Stormberg, having to retire with the loss of over 600 men captured.

On the receipt of news of the capture of the battalions at Ladysmith orders were at once given for the despatch of further reinforcements from England, and it was subsequently decided to send out two new divisions in addition to the Army Corps. The repulses experienced early in December made it necessary to take further measures. On the 5th of the month it was announced that Field-Marshal Lord Roberts would go out to take supreme command at the Cape, leaving Sir R. Buller to confine his attention to the operations in Natal; Lord Kitchener was appointed Chief of the Staff to Lord Roberts. Large reinforcements were ordered out from England, and employment at the front was offered both to the Yeomanry and to the Volunteers, while portions of the Militia were invited to volunteer for duty abroad and in South Africa. These calls were eagerly responded to. At the same time the further help offered by Australia and Canada was accepted, and preparations for sending mounted troops were actively pressed on in the different Colonies.

The effects of the war have, of course, been greatly felt in South Africa, where trade has been completely disorganised and industry brought to a standstill, while the arrival of large numbers of refugees from the Rand has taxed local charity to the utmost, despite the funds raised in this country for the relief of distress. But the loss and suffering in Natal have been specially great since that colony has been the scene of the principal warfare, and the pillaging and destruction of property by the invading Boers has added to the damage entailed by the suspension of business. These hardships have, however, been borne with the greatest steadfastness, and the Colony has cheerfully made every sacrifice to assist the Imperial troops.

Under Cape Colony it may be mentioned that on the 30th December, 1898, an Act was passed giving to the naval authorities the control of the port of Simon's Bay, with powers to carry out extensive works, including a graving dock. These rights had been sought for several years. Elections were held in the Spring under the Redistribution Act, 1898, the result being that Mr. Schreiner continued in power with a slightly increased majority.

In Natal the Prime Minister Sir H. Binns, died on the 6th of June, and a new Ministry was formed by Colonel Hime.

In December, 1898, the detailed claim of the South African Republic for damages for Dr. Jameson's raid was received, the total of which was £1,677,938 3s. 3d., including the sum of £1,000,000 for moral or intellectual damage which the Republic continued to press. The claim was forwarded to the British South Africa Company, who proposed that the claim for material damages should with certain limitations be referred to arbitration. Mr. Chamberlain accordingly directed the High Commissioner in May to forward the Company's reply to the Government of the South African Republic, at the same time expressing his opinion that it was fair and reasonable, but again intimating that the claim for moral and intellectual damage could not be considered. The arrangements for arbitration were not, however, made when war broke out.

St. Helena was brought into telegraphic communication by the laying of a new cable from the Cape by the associated Eastern companies. The line was continued from St. Helena to Ascension, and by taking a deep sea route, remote from the causes of interruptions experienced on the West Coast lines, will no doubt, when complete, add greatly to the security of communication between this country and South Africa.

Commercially, the history of Canada during 1889 has been one of unbroken prosperity. The International Commission for the settlement of outstanding questions between Canada and the United States continued its work in the early part of the year. The deliberations were confidential, but the Protocol of the final meeting in February was published. Shortly after the final meeting, when the Commission adjourned with the intention of meeting again at Ottawa in August, Lord Herschell, the chief British representative, died at Washington. Negotiations with regard to the Alaska Boundary, which had occupied a large part of the deliberations of the Commission, were continued between the Governments of Great Britain and Canada and the United States Government, and an agreement was arrived at in October for a provisional boundary in the neighborhood of the Lynn Canal. Sir Louis Davies, Minister of Marine and Fisheries, accompanied by Mr. Pope, Under Secretary of State, visited England in September in connection with these negotiations. The question of a final settlement is still under discussion between the Governments concerned. No definite arrangement has yet been come to in the matter of a fast Atlantic service between Great Britain and Canada; Mr. Dobell, of the Canadian Cabinet, has visited England in connection with the project.
of an outbreak of war with the Transvaal a number of offers were received from Volunteers in Canada, and the Dominion Government offered the services of 1,000 men, who were equipped and despatched with remarkable celerity, and left amidst great demonstrations of loyalty. It was arranged in the case of the Canadian contingent, as also with regard to the Australian and New Zealand contingents, that the Colonial Governments should equip and transport the men to South Africa, and that the Imperial Government should pay them at Army rates from the date of disembarkation, should pay wound pensions, etc., and should provide for their transport to their own Colony on the conclusion of the war.

On the loss of two battalions at Ladysmith at the end of October, a further offer of 1,000 men was made by Canada, but Her Majesty's Government in grateful terms declined it for the time being. In December, after the reverses experienced by the British forces at Magersfontein and Colenso, the offer was accepted.

The history of Newfoundland during 1899 has been uneventful. The report of the Royal Commission which visited the Colony in 1898 was presented in March. It is still under the consideration of Her Majesty's Government, and has not yet been published.

In Australia public interest was centred throughout the year in the question of Federation, and the movement at last reached a favourable conclusion. At the end of 1898 the failure of the Draft Bill to secure acceptance by the requisite number of voters in New South Wales, and the objections of the Legislature of that Colony to certain provisions of the Bill, appeared likely to prove a serious obstacle to further progress. But at a meeting of the Prime Ministers of all the Australian Colonies at Melbourne, in January and February, 1899, amendments to meet the views of New South Wales were quickly agreed upon. It was arranged that after the Draft Commonwealth Bill, as amended, had been accepted by the Parliament of New South Wales, it should be referred to the electors of that Colony, and, if adopted by them, should then be considered in the other Colonies. South Australia, however, for purposes of local convenience, was to be at liberty to take the referendum upon the Bill on the occasion of the General Election without waiting for New South Wales.

In South Australia, accordingly, an Act to amend the Federal Enabling Act of 1895 was passed in March, and the vote was taken at the end of April, resulting in a large majority for the amended Bill. In New South Wales, after a conflict between the two Houses of the Legislature, which was ended by the addition of twelve new members to the Upper House, an amended Federal Enabling Act was passed in April, without alteration of the arrangements agreed upon by the Premiers, except the additional provision that eight weeks should elapse before the referendum was taken. On the 20th of June the amended Commonwealth Bill was submitted to the popular vote and accepted by a large majority.

In the course of July, Victoria and Tasmania passed Acts amending the Enabling Acts of 1896, and the Commonwealth Bill was accepted by overwhelming majorities of the electors. In Queensland, where no legislative action had previously been completed, an Enabling Act was passed in June, and on the referendum being taken the Bill was accepted by a majority of the electorate.

In Western Australia the matter was brought before the Legislature, and the provisions of the Bill discussed. The West Australian Enabling Act of 1896 had differed from the similar Acts in other Colonies, by providing that the Commonwealth Bill as finally adopted by the delegates charged with framing it should be approved by Parliament before submission to the electors (though, in view of the vote of New South Wales in 1898, no definite action was taken on the draft as settled by the Convention at the Melbourne sitting). The Prime Minister was, however, informed by the Prime Ministers of the other Federating Colonies that no further amendments of the Bill could then be considered. In November the Legislative Council of Western Australia decided against a referendum being taken.

Addresses to the Queen, praying that the Commonwealth Bill may be passed into law by the Imperial Parliament, have been received from the Parliaments of New South Wales, Victoria, South Australia, Tasmania, and Queensland, and the measure came before Her Majesty's Government with a view to its submission to Parliament in the forthcoming session.

With the exception of the notable changes in Ministry in most of the Colonies in the latter half of the year, there is little to call for special mention in the Australian Colonies during 1899. The generous offers of troops for service in South Africa is recorded elsewhere, and it is only necessary to mention here the extraordinary enthusiasm and loyalty which marked the departure of the contingents both in Australia and New Zealand.

In New South Wales the Ministry of Mr. G. H. Reid was defeated in the Legislative Assembly in August, and tendered their resignation. They were succeeded by a Ministry formed by Mr. Lyne, who had resumed the leadership of the Opposition on the retirement of Mr. Barton after the Federation measure (of which he was an ardent supporter) had been secured.

In Tasmania the Ministry of Sir Edward Braddon resigned in October, on defeat in the Assembly, and was succeeded by a Ministry under the leadership of Mr. N. F. Lewis.

In Queensland Mr. Dickson, who succeeded to the Premiership on the death of Mr. Byrnes, resigned office in November, and a Ministry was formed by Mr. Dawson; but he was immediately defeated in the Assembly and a fresh Ministry was formed by Mr. Philip, Treasurer in Mr. Dickson's Cabinet, and Mr. Dickson resumed his post of Chief Secretary.

In South Australia a vote of no confidence was carried in the Assembly by a majority of one; Mr. Kingston then resigned office, which he had held since 1893, and a Ministry was formed by Mr. Solomon. But Mr. Solomon was unable to retain office, and Mr. Holder, Treasurer in Mr. Kingston's Administration, became Premier.

In Victoria also a change of Ministry occurred, Sir George Turner being defeated in the Assembly. He was succeeded by Mr. McLean.

In British New Guinea the new Lieutenant-Governor, Mr. Le Hunte, arrived early in the year and at once took up the question of land grants and the consideration of the financial arrangements. On the latter point the contributing Colonies sanctioned considerable augmentations of expenditure required for the extension of the Administration, to be met from the Accumulated Revenue Fund. Mr. Le Hunte's proposals for settling the land question were accepted by the Prime Ministers, and an
Ordinance was drafted for giving effect to them. During the year the Lieutenant Governor made tours in almost every part of the Possession.

New Zealand's generous offer of troops for service in the Transvaal is recorded under the South African heading. They were despatched with remarkable celerity, amid scenes of patriotic enthusiasm.

In Fiji the increase of revenue has been maintained, and considerable sums have been available for public works, the expenditure on which had during the years of depression been reduced to the smallest proportions. The works in progress include improvements in water supply and other sanitary measures for the benefit of the native population, and also road-making; and provision has been made for the renewal and extension of Suva Wharf and for necessary new buildings. An attempt is also being made to arrest the decrease of the native population and improve their condition by the appointment of provincial inspectors, who are dealing with the questions of better sanitation, better organization of labour, a more equitable system of refunding to the natives the value of the produce paid to the Government in excess of taxes, and the mitigation of the effects of the communal custom of joint property; and provincial hospitals are being established and new medical officers appointed to deal with the needs of outlying districts for medical treatment and supervision of sanitation.

In Malta bills were introduced to remove the injustice of a British subject, unfamiliar with the Italian language, being tried by a court of justice in a British Colony in a language (Italian) which he could not understand and which is not the native language of the country, and to give a British subject facilities for the conduct of civil proceedings to which he is a party in the English language. These bills being rejected by the Council of Government, an Order in Council was issued in March containing provisions similar to those of the bills; and notice was given by local proclamation of the intention of Her Majesty's Government that, after fifteen years, the English language should be substituted for the Italian in all legal proceedings. The action of the elected members of the Council also made it necessary to issue an Order in Council in July to enable the Government of Malta to meet its obligations in regard to the loan to be raised for the purpose of drainage works.

In Gibraltar the drainage works have been completed, and steady progress made with the harbour works.

In Cyprus the irrigation works have made good progress; those at Synkraisi have been completed, and a large scheme for the irrigation of the Messoria Plain has already been taken in hand. The total expenditure sanctioned for the works is £60,000. By the Colonial Loans Act of 1898 Parliament authorized a loan to Cyprus of £34,000, (including the sum above mentioned), and it is hoped that the construction of a harbour at Famagusta will shortly be proceeded with. A railway from Famagusta to Nicosia has also been started, but the completion of this work will be deferred until the completion of the proposed harbour is sufficiently advanced to enable the two works to be completed simultaneously. Further progress has been made in the construction of roads, and the cultivation of carobs and olives has been greatly extended by grafting large numbers of wild trees in the Government forests. Measures continue to be taken to instruct the peasantry in improved methods of cultivation, and efforts are also being made to improve the breed of horses, cattle, and donkeys by the importation of pedigree animals. A new Tariff Law has been passed, under which the customs duties have been re-arranged, the tithes on olives, olive oil, and cotton seed abolished, and specific export duties substituted for titles with regard to a number of articles, and thus the policy of relieving the peasantry by lightening the taxes on minor industries has been further carried out. A mail contract for a weekly service with Egypt has been entered into with the Austrian Lloyd Company and the service has been running for some months.

The year 1898 has seen peace completely restored in the Sierra Leone Protectorate, after the disturbances of the previous year. The last phase of the movement took place when, in December, 1898, patrol columns were sent through the length and breadth of the Protectorate with the object of establishing the authority of the Government throughout by a demonstration of force. The expedition rendered additional service by driving back across the frontier and severely punishing the Kissi tribe, who raided the Protectorate in January from the north of Liberia, but have since given no further trouble. In January the late Sir David Chalmers sent in his report upon the disturbances in 1898, in which he argued against the continuation of the hut tax; it was, however, considered desirable to retain it, and the collection has proceeded quietly in the districts where it is levied.

Continuous progress has been made during the year in the Sierra Leone Railway. On the 1st of May the section from Freetown to Songo-town—the first line to be completed in the British West African Colonies—was opened for traffic. The line is now being constructed as far as Rotofunk, and an extension of it beyond that place is under consideration.

Crops were again good in the Gambia, and this Colony's prosperity continues. A large surplus was realised in 1898, and several public works are in contemplation.

The Gold Coast had a very prosperous year, but will have to meet heavy charges on account of the Northern Territories for some years to come. The construction of the railway from Sekondi to Takoradi is under progress. The telegraph line has been extended to Wa, in the Northern territories. Efforts are being made to encourage the cultivation of coffee and cocoa, and free instruction is given in the methods to be employed. A bill to regulate concessions of land and mining rights, and to constitute a Concessions Court, has been prepared for the consideration of the local legislature. The Colony has been quiet on the whole, but there were some disturbances in Wani, due to tribal quarrels early in the year, and it was necessary to send a detachment of the Hausa Constabulary against the Prafras in July. This expedition was completely successful.

During the year the administration of the Northern Territories was further organised by Lieutenant Colonel H. P. Northcott. The Colony has sustained a great loss by his subsequent death in the action on the Moider River.

In Lagos a Protectorate has been formed by Order in Council, subject to all treaty rights, over all the territories up to the boundaries of Southern Nigeria, Northern Nigeria, and Dahomey. The railway reached Abeokuta in March, and has been progressing towards Ibadan.
As to the Niger Territories, the Colonial Office was occupied throughout the year with the business connected with the taking over of the administration from the Royal Niger Company. After considerable negotiations, an arrangement was concluded in June between the Treasury and the Company, under which, subject to the sanction of Parliament, it was agreed that the Charter of the Company should be revoked; and that the Company should be relieved of its administrative powers and duties, and should assign to Her Majesty's Government the benefit of all its treaties and all its lands, but should retain its plant and trading assets, stations, waterside depôts, buildings, wharves, and workshops. The lands so assigned embraced not only the vast territories over which the administrative control had been obtained by treaty, but also those, covering considerable distances on both banks of the Niger, of which the private ownership had been acquired by agreement. For this assignment it was agreed that Her Majesty's Government should assume the liability for the interest (12,500l. a year) payable on the public debt (250,000l.) of the Company, and should pay to the Company 450,000l. Certain materials and stores were also to be taken over for the sum of 115,000l. The money was voted by Parliament near the end of the Session, and the three months' notice which had been agreed upon was given to the Company on the 1st of October, so that the Royal Charter of the Company could be revoked on the 1st of January, 1900, and Her Majesty's Government could then enter upon the administration of the territories. The intended transfer of the administration, however, did not interfere with the Company as a trading corporation, and only that part of its local staff and assets could be handed over to Her Majesty's Government which was not required by it in that capacity; it was, therefore, necessary to consider from the commencement of the year what officials, and what buildings, materials, and stores could be taken over for the new administration, and what would be the further requirements. Inventories were accordingly made out of such buildings, &c., of the Company as it seemed desirable to acquire, and the price was settled as above stated; but for the purposes of effective and progressive administration, especially in the Northern territories, in which little had hitherto been done, it was necessary to make further provision, and, in addition to certain expenditure on boats and vessels, the Colonial Office was authorised to spend 35,000l. for temporary buildings, workshops, stores, &c. The character of the country and climate makes it practically necessary to send out from this country at present all the houses (wooden), and nearly all the foodstuffs and other requirements of Europeans, and the difficulty and cost of sending up these supplies are greatly enhanced by the uncertainties of navigation on the Niger and the fact that it is only available for such purposes, except at great risk, for about half the year. That part of the Company's territories which is to the south of Iddah is added to what was the Niger Coast Protectorate, and by an Order in Council issued at the end of the year the combined territory is called the Protectorate of Southern Nigeria, and placed under the administration of a High Commissioner, who will have power to legislate by proclamation; a similar Order in Council was issued at the same time constituting the territories north of Iddo the Protectorate of Northern Nigeria, also under the administration of a High Commissioner, and with similar powers. In the former province the customs revenue collected on the coast form a means ready at hand towards meeting new requirements; but in Northern Nigeria this revenue is not available, as it is intended that imports which have paid customs duties at British ports on the coast shall be free to enter Northern Nigeria without further payment. Imperial funds have, therefore, been provided to initiate the departments, including those for public works and the marine flotilla, required to begin the administration of Northern Nigeria, and it is hoped, as peace and order are gradually secured along the rivers, the abundant trade from the teeming Hausa towns, which has for generations gone across the desert to Tripoli and Egypt, will come the comparatively short route to the waterways, and thence to British steamers. In Northern Nigeria Col. F. D. Lugard, C.B., D.S.O., previously Commissioner and Commandant of the West African Frontier Force, has been appointed the High Commissioner, and it is intended to appoint under him three political residents in charge of districts. In Southern Nigeria, Sir R. D. R. Moor, K.C.M.G., previously the Commissioner and Consul-General of the Niger Coast Protectorate, has been appointed the High Commissioner, and the Province has been divided into four divisions under four divisional commissioners.

Col. J. Willcocks, C.M.G., D.S.O., previously second in command of the West African Frontier Force, was appointed Commandant in place of Col. Lugard. No important expedition was found necessary during the year, but the force was brought to a very efficient condition, and the work accomplished reflects great credit on the officers concerned.

A conference was held at Brussels in the spring with a view to concerted international action for the increase of the Spirit Duties on the West Coast. Under the Brussels General Act, 1890, a minimum duty, equivalent to 6½d. per gallon, was provided for on all spirits imported into the territories from 20° N. lat. to 22° S. lat., and it was further agreed that the Powers should prohibit the importation of spirits in the districts of this zone where, "either on account of religious belief or from other motives," their use does not exist or has not been developed. The British, German, and French colonies have levied much higher rates than the above minimum; and at the recent conference the minimum was raised to a rate equivalent to about 3s. per proof gallon, except in Dahomey and Togoland, where it will be about 2s. 6d.

On the invitation of Mr. Chamberlain, the Committee of Management of the Seamen's Hospital Society established a School of Tropical Medicine at the Seamen's Hospital Society's Branch Hospital, near the Royal Victoria and Albert Docks, E.; and the medical officers appointed to Crown Colonies are, whenever possible, sent to this school to undergo a course of instruction with regard to tropical diseases. A school for similar purposes was established by local enterprise at Liverpool.

The Colonial Office and the Royal Society co-operated to send out a commission to study Malarial Diseases, and members of the Commission have visited Blantyre and Freetown. The Liverpool School also sent out a Mission under Major R. Ross for the same purpose, with the result that the germs of malaria were discovered in the species of mosquito called anopholes.

In the West Indian Islands the position during the year showed a slight improvement owing chiefly to a rise in the prices of cocoa and sugar, which last was largely due to the action of the United States in imposing countervailing duties upon bounty-fed sugar.
The question of central factories made some progress during the year, and an exhaustive report on the position in Antigua was drawn up by Mr. Robert Harvey and submitted for the consideration of the Secretary of State.

At the beginning of the summer, negotiations for the conclusion of reciprocity conventions between the United States of America and the West Indies were reopened on the basis of a reduction of 12½ per cent. on the United States duty on sugar and molasses, in return for counterbalancing reductions of duty on imports from the United States, mainly foodstuffs. Eventually conventions were signed on behalf of British Guiana, Jamaica, and Trinidad, to be ratified if the Colonies concerned agreed to accept the Conventions, and if the United States Senate also consented. The Legislature of Trinidad, however, decided that the Colony could not accept the Convention in view of the loss of revenue involved. A similar Convention was also negotiated on behalf of the Turks and Caicos Islands, on the basis of a 12½ per cent. reduction of the United States duty on salt, etc., in return for various reductions of duties on United States products, and a further Convention was arranged on behalf of Bermuda.

It was found possible to assent to the introduction of an increased number of immigrants into Trinidad and British Guiana, and a considerable number were recruited during the year for Jamaica also.

Negotiations for the establishment of a direct steamer service between Jamaica and the United Kingdom proceeded during the year, and an agreement was signed with the Jamaica Produce and Transport Association, which however proved abortive owing to the failure of the Company to raise the necessary capital. A contract was signed with Messrs. Pickford and Black for an accelerated and improved service between the West Indies and Canada. The service is to commence on the 1st July, 1900, and the subsidy of 27,000l. per annum is to be paid in equal proportions by the Imperial Government and the Dominion of Canada.

The general position of Jamaica showed a satisfactory improvement during the year. A Report of Sir David Barbour, K.C.S.I., on the condition of the island was received and considered, and certain measures for reducing expenditure, increasing revenue, and adjusting the finances generally were recommended to the Colonial Government. It was considered advisable to instruct the Governor to fill up the full number of nominated members of the Legislative Council provided for under the Constitution of the Colony.

A reform was introduced into the constitution of the Federal Council of the Leeward Islands, under which it was made to consist of eight official and eight non-official and nominated members, and a casting vote was given to the President.

The work of settling small holders in St. Vincent on lands purchased from the Imperial Grant made in 1898 for that purpose proceeded steadily during the year, and a large number of allotments were surveyed and readily taken up by peasants.

On the 8th of August a destructive hurricane visited the Leeward Islands and subsequently the Bahamas, and on the 14th of September the former colony suffered additional damage from another storm. A Mansion House Relief Fund was opened, and a sum of about 6,000l. subscribed and remitted to the Leeward Islands, where the islands of Montserrat and Nevis had suffered most severely. The Imperial Government subsequently made a free grant of 6,000l. to the Colonial Government to be expended in loans to planters in Montserrat and Nevis to enable them to repair the works on their estates and give employment to labourers so as to lessen the necessity for continued relief works.

In the Falkland Islands there were re-arrangements of the tariff, and a small export tax on sheep's wool and hides was imposed, the latter measure having proved necessary in order to effect an equilibrium between the revenue and expenditure and to provide the means of wiping off the deficit which had accumulated during the past few years.

The final decision by arbitration during this year of the long-standing boundary dispute between the Colony of British Guiana and the Republic of Venezuela was an event of unusual importance not only in its bearing on the interests of the Colony, but as closing finally an incident which, less than four years previously, had given rise to considerable feeling in the United Kingdom and the United States.

The treaty between Great Britain and Venezuela for the arbitration of the question was signed on 2nd February, 1897; the ratifications were exchanged some months later, and the submission of the printed cases and arguments for which the treaty provided was completed by the close of 1898. In January, 1899, the preliminary meeting of the arbitral tribunal was held in Paris; it was not a meeting of the full court, and merely took preliminary steps to arrange procedure. The full court met at Paris on the 15th of June. The President of the Court was His Excellency M. de Martens, Councillor of the Russian Empire; Lord Russell of Killowen, Lord Chief Justice of England, and Lord Justice Henn Collins were the members nominated by the Privy Council on behalf of Great Britain, and the Hon. Melville Fuller, Chief Justice of the United States, and Mr. Justice Brewer were the members nominated by the Supreme Court of the United States on behalf of Venezuela. Of these Lord Russell took the place of the late Lord Herschell, whose name stands in the treaty.

The early sittings of the Court were broken up by the constant absence of the President, whose presence was required at the Peace Conference then proceeding at the Hague, but with these exceptions the Court sat de die in diem from the 15th June to the end of September. The order of speeches was arranged by consent, and no inference was to be drawn from it. The Attorney-General of England, Sir Richard Webster, opened the argument in a speech which lasted 13 days, putting in the most material documents out of the vast masses of evidence which had been accumulated. Mr. Mallet Prevost, one of the American Counsel replied, claiming that Venezuela was entitled by virtue of the early Spanish title to all the country as far as the Essequibo river as her eastern boundary. He was followed by Mr. Soley, who dealt with the events of the nineteenth century only. Their speeches lasted some 20 days. Sir Robert Reid, replying for Great Britain, delivered a short but clear and incisive argument; other counsel on each side followed, and the concluding speeches were delivered by the Attorney-General and General Harrison, formerly President of the United States.

The dispute over this boundary had begun as soon as the Dutch and Spaniards had come close to each other in Guiana, but neither side had endeavoured to obtain a formal settlement, and it was a legacy
left to Great Britain and Venezuela. In 1840 Sir R. Schomburgk was sent out to British Guiana to survey the boundaries of the Colony with a view to the settlement of all disputes by treaty. He surveyed and proposed a line which seemed to offer every advantage to both countries. The Republic of Venezuela, however, persisted in claiming almost the whole of the old Dutch Colony of Essequibo, and declined to consider any reasonable compromise. This extreme claim to the line of the Essequibo itself was always balanced by the extreme claims of Great Britain to the whole basin of the western tributaries of the Essequibo; but whereas Great Britain in the arbitral proceedings followed the precedent set by successive Secretaries of State, and forbore to press their extreme claim, the Venezuelan commissioners for the first time that the line was drawn by British commissioners, insisted rigidly upon Schomburgk's line as representing the fair and natural boundary between the Colony and the Republic; this line began beyond Barima Point, close to the mouth of the Orinoco, but the possession of Barima Point had not of late years been pressed by Great Britain.

The decision of the tribunal was delivered on 3rd October, 1899, and assigned all the territory east of Schomburgk's line to Great Britain, except a piece at the mouth of the Barima and a small area inland between the Wenami and the upper reach of the Cayuni.

The railway to NYLON showed no signs of a decrease during 1899. It was decided to proceed with the construction of the northern extension of the Schomburg-Kurunegala railway, which is to be carried to the Jaffna Peninsula. A light railway from Nann Oya to Uda Pussellawa was also authorised. The development of plumbago mining has been phenomenally rapid, owing to the great increase in the demand for the mineral, and regulations for the management of the industry have engaged the attention of the Government.

The taking over of the new territory on the mainland of Hong Kong was not effected without resistance on the part of Chinese rioters, which had to be quelled by the local military and naval forces. The Colonial Volunteers distinguished themselves in these operations. Sporadic cases of plague showed themselves in March, and developed into an epidemic, which died down towards the end of the year.

There was a serious outbreak of plague in MAURITIUS. The financial situation showed every sign of improvement, as there was an exceptionally good sugar crop.

The STRAITS SETTLEMENTS maintained their high level of prosperity. It was decided to construct a railway across the island of Singapore. The Colony lost an able and public-spirited Governor in Sir Charles Macleod, who died suddenly in September.

The FEDERATED MALAY STATES continue to develop steadily in every direction.

The revenue of SEYCHELLES for 1899 bids fair to exceed all previous returns, thanks to the favourable state of the vanilla trade.

Among the movements of the year which have general Colonial interest may be mentioned the progress of the scheme for laying a British Pacific cable and the extension of the Imperial Penny Post and of the cheaper Parcel Post system.

The PACIFIC CABLE PROJECT, reported on by the Committee of 1897, was advanced by the proposal of the Colonial Office, instead of an arrangement for the joint ownership and control by the Imperial and Colonial Governments of the cable, as recommended by the Committee; the Imperial Government to guarantee five-eighteenths of any loss and to receive the same proportion of any profits, the Colonies taking the other thirteen-eighteenths. In reply to this, Her Majesty's Government proposed that Canada and Australasia should raise the funds, and construct and work the cable, and that the Treasury should contribute an annual subsidy for 20 years of five-eighteenths of any loss, the amount of such contribution not to exceed £20,000. This proposal left any profits to the Colonies, but it was objected to by Canada, principally on the grounds of the colonial losses. Her Majesty's Government did not join in the scheme, would be obliged to a heavier charge, and that the cable would not have the character of an Imperial work. Her Majesty's Government accordingly agreed to consider the matter on the basis of utilising the credit of the United Kingdom in providing the capital; and it was arranged at a conference held on 4th July that the elaboration of the scheme and the management of the line should be entrusted to a Board of eight members, three, including the chairman, representing the Home Government, three Australasian, and two Canada. In November, the following members were appointed: The Earl of Selborne, Sir F. Mowatt (chairman), and Sir G. H. Murray (Imperial); the Earl of Aberdeen, and Lord Strathcona (Canadian); and Sir J. Salomons, Sir A. Clarke, and Mr. W. F. Reid (Australia).

BAHAMAS.

Situation and Area.

The Bahamas, the most northerly of the British West Indian Colonies, are a chain of coral islands lying between 21° 42' and 27° 34' N. lat., and 72° 40' and 79° 5' W. long., composed of about 20 inhabited islands, and an immense number of islets and rocks. The principal islands are New Providence (containing the capital, Nassau), Abaco, Harbour Island, Eleuthera, Inagua, Mayaguana, Ragged Island, Rum Cay, Exuma, Long Island, Long Cay, and the Bimins, all of which are ports of entry; and Great Bahama, Crooked Island, Acklin Island, Cat Island, Watling's Island, once known as St. Salvador, the Berry Islands, and Andros Island (containing the only river). The total area is 4,466 square miles, or about half the size of Wales.

History.

St. Salvador, so-called by Columbus, the native name being Guanahani, one of the islands composing this chain, was the first land discovered by him on his voyage in 1492. A few years later all the Carib inhabitants were transported to work in the Cuba mines, and the islands were abandoned. They were included in the charter given by Queen Elizabeth to Sir Humphrey Gilbert in 1578, but no visit was made to them or occupation effected, and in 1612 they were nominally attached to Virginia. Settlers from the Bermudas found their way in considerable numbers to Eleuthera, in 1646, and in 1666, some years later, also to New Providence. This latter island, and all the others between 22° and 27° N. lat. were granted by Charles II to a proprietary body in 1670, and in 1671 Captain Johnson Wentworth was appointed by the proprietors to be their first Governor. No regular system of government appears to have been established however, and New Providence continued to be more or less merely a shelter for pirates and a disorderly set of people. It was laid waste by the Spaniards in 1680 or 1682, and in 1763 the French and Spaniards combined annihilated the settlement. After this it became a regular rendezvous for pirates, who were finally extirpated in 1718 by the English, under Captain Woodes Rogers, and a regular administration formed and colonists introduced, including a considerable number of Germans from the Palatinate. In 1781 the Bahamas were surrendered to the Spaniards, but at the conclusion of the war they were once more annexed by Great Britain, which was confirmed in their possession at the Peace of Versailles, 1783.

In 1848 the Turks and Caicos Islands, which geographically form part of the Bahamas chain, were separated from the other Bahamas, and formed into a distinct Presidency, under the Government-in-Chief of the Governor of Jamaica.

Climate and Inhabitants.

The climate is salubrious and very pleasant in the winter season, and the Colony has in recent years been much frequented by visitors from the United States and Canada—there being excellent hotels and other accommodation for tourists. The annual rainfall is 45 inches, the rainy season extending from June to October. The mean temperature is 79°-5 degrees, the extreme range being from 54°-7 to 96°-2.

The majority of the inhabitants are of the negro race. About one quarter are of European descent: English is universally spoken.

Trade and Industry.

The commercial relations of the Colony are mainly with the United States. Considerable quantities of pine-apples and oranges are exported. In 1896 the value of oranges, lemons, &c., and other fruits was £4,586l.; in 1898 £4,197,620 pine-apples were exported, valued at £24,360l.

Cotton, the cultivation of which was introduced by Loyalist refugees from the United States, was grown in large quantities prior to the abolition of slavery, and also during the American War but has ceased to be a staple. The cotton exported in 1898 was only valued at £143l.

The cultivation and preparation of the sisal fibre plant has been stimulated recently and the quantity and value exported in 1898 was 1,251,736 lbs. in value £14,714l. The area planted at the end of 1896 was 20,000 acres.

The sugar-cane grows luxuriantly in many of the islands, but is little cultivated.

The Colony enjoyed great prosperity during the American Civil War, when it was the headquarters of many blockade running operations.

Fishing is extensively carried on, over 100 native-built boats, with 500 men, being employed. Shells and pearls are largely exported. Sponge-fishing employs a large fleet, 97,412l. worth being shipped in 1898. Nassau is a port of registry, and had on 31st December, 1898, 623 ships registered, of 22,112 tons.

Salt-raking, one of the earliest industries, has fallen off of late, the export of salt in 1898 being only 800l., as compared with 2,470l. in 1890. Some of the islets yield guano. The chief imports are textile fabrics, bread stuffs, spirits, and wines.

Lighthouses on several of the islands have been established, and are maintained, by the Imperial Government at a cost of £13,000l. per annum, exclusive of stores supplied from England.

Currency and Banking.

The legal tender currency is British sterling, United States current coin, silver of the Latin Union, and gold doublemints. Accounts are kept in sterling. There is no Colonial currency. A local bank, called the Bank of Nassau, was established on 1st June, 1889. It had on 31st December, 1898, a note issue of 5,500l., and deposits amounting to 43,000l. A Post Office Savings Bank was established in January, 1886, and had on 31st December, 1898, 10,415l. deposited.

Means of Communication.

There are no railways or telegraphs in the Colony, and but few good roads except in New Providence. There is regular fortnightly mail communication with New York and Cuba, and frequent vessels to and from Cuba and Key West. Till February, 1892, the nearest point in telegraphic communication with Europe was Key West, but in that month a cable from Nassau to Florida was completed. The rates of postage are:

Constitution.

The Executive Government is conducted, under Letters Patent, by the Governor aided by an Executive Council of 9 members. The Legislative authority resides in the Governor, a Legislative Council of 9 members, nominated by the Crown and a Representative Assembly of 29 members, elected for 14 districts by persons owning land of the value of £5, or occupying houses of the rental value of £2, 8s. in New Providence, or half that amount in the outlying islands. The qualifications of Electors are full age, a residence of 12 months, with land value £5; or being a householder of premises value £2, 8s. in New Providence, or £1, 4s. elsewhere, for six months. The qualification of Members is possession of an estate of real or personal property of the value of £200. The Executive Council is composed partly of official and partly of unofficial Members, who have a seat in one of the branches of the Legislature.

Education.

There is a Government system of elementary education, established 1847, and modified by laws of 1864, 1875, 1885, 1886, 1888, and 1889. The central control is in a Board of Education nominated by the Governor. Local Committees, partly elected, exercise local supervision only.

There are 44 unsectarian Government schools, with 5,998 scholars; 11 aided schools, with 981 scholars; 31 Church of England and 33 private schools, with 2,166 scholars. The Government schools were made free in 1885. The compulsory clauses of the law are enforced only in Nassau and the larger villages. Higher education is provided at the Nassau Grammar School, the Queen's College, and St. Hilda's School, all in Nassau.

BARBADOS.

Situation and Area.

Barbados is situated in latitude 13° 4' North and longitude 59° 37' West, and is the most easterly of the Caribbean Islands. It is nearly 21 miles long by 14 in breadth, and contains an area of 106,470 acres, or about 166 square miles, a little larger than Rutland.

History.

The exact date of the discovery of Barbados is not known. It is said to have been first visited by the Portuguese, who finding it uninhabited and rude in appearance, named the isle Los Barbudos, from the number of bearded fig-trees which they found. It was nominally taken possession of by the English ship "Olive" in 1605, when it was almost uninhabited. In 1625 Sir William Courteen, a London merchant, under the protection of the Earl of Marlborough, who held a grant of the island from James I, fitted out two large ships, only one of which arrived at Barbados, and the party, which consisted of some thirty persons, landed on the leeward side of the island formed a town called James' (or Hole) Town, and appointed Captain William Deane their governor. In 1627 the Earl of Carlisle obtained a grant from Charles I of all the Caribbean Islands. This grant was opposed by the former patentee, Lord Marlborough, but the matter was compromised on the Earl of Carlisle agreeing to settle on the Earl of Marlborough an annuity of 300l. Soon after this the Earl of Carlisle being employed on a diplomatic mission, the Earl of Pembroke, then Lord Chamberlain, obtained a revocation of the former nobleman's patent in his favour and supported Sir W. Courteen; but on the Earl of Carlisle's return from his embassy, he remonstrated with the king, who reinstated him in possession of the territory. Woolerstone, a native of Bermuda, was then commissioned by the Earl of Carlisle as governor, and in 1628 sixty-four settlers arrived in Carlisle Bay, commenced the erection of wooden houses, threw a bridge across the river which intersected the ground, and laid the foundation of Bridgetown, the present capital. The leeward and windward men opposed each other, the latter ultimately triumphing. The civil war which raged in England contributed to people and enrich the island; and on the downfall of Charles, many families attached to the Royal cause found shelter in Barbados. The island was afterwards governed by Lord Willoughby, a Royalist, to whom it was conveyed by Lord Carlisle (son of the first patentee); but when the island was subdued by the Commonwealth he was banished. In 1682, after the Restoration, Lord Willoughby renewed his claim, and the kinsmen and heirs of the two earls brought forward demands on the settlers. To satisfy these claims, a duty of 4½ per cent. on all exports was imposed; and under certain conditions the proprietary government was dissolved and the sovereignty of Barbados annexed to the British Crown. The inhabitants long protested against the imposition of the 4½ per cent. duties, but without success; and it was not till 1838, four years after the abolition of slavery, that the tax was abolished by an Act of Parliament.

Barbados has not, like most of the neighbouring islands, changed owners; it has always remained in possession of Great Britain.

General Description.

Bridgetown, the chief town and port, is situated in the parish of St. Michael, in latitude 13° 5' 42" North, and longitude 59° 38' 29" West. This town contains, according to the census of 1891, 21,000 inhabitants. Speightstown, the only other town, has about 1,500 inhabitants.

Carlisle Bay, the harbour of Barbados, is an open roadstead, much exposed to the wind from the south and south-west. There is an inner harbour or careenage, protected by a structure called the Mole Head. It is a port of registry, and had registered on 31st December, 1898, 47 vessels, of a total net tonnage of 7,372 tons.

The island is almost encircled by coral reefs, which in some parts, as off the parish of St. Phillip, extend nearly 3 miles to seaward, and prove very dangerous to navigation.

A geological map, with explanatory memoir of the island, was published in 1891 by Messrs. J. B. Harrison and A. J. Jukes Brown, which shows that that area of the island called the Scotland district, which is the part enclosed by a semicircular sweep of the ridge in the north-east, is composed of sandstones, clays, and insular earths, the products of which may be in future a valuable source of revenue to the island; already excellent fire-bricks are made near the end of the railway.

In Schomburgk's history of Barbados there is a short reference to the deposit of asphaltum found in the island, and Messrs. A. J. Jukes Browne and J. B. Harrison casually mention it as occurring occasionally in small quantities, which planters have attempted to burn under their sugar boilers, but not with sufficient success to lead to its general use. In 1893 an American named Julius Pinney suggested to Mr. Walter Merivale, M.I.C.E., late managing director of the Barbados Railway, the possibility of mining it for commercial purposes. A mine was opened by Mr. Merivale on the College Estate in January, 1896, from which about 500 tons of the purest asphaltum were extracted during the year 1898. Other mines have since been opened, and in 1898 the total amount of manjak exported from the island amounted to 1,160 tons. The market is gradually opening to this new product, and prices are obtained varying from 2l. to 7l. a ton. There appears to be a demand for it in the following trades: varnish making, gas making, electric cable insulating, asphalt paving, &c. It seems probable that the deposits extend under the coral in all parts of the island.

Much of the geological information concerning the coral area was obtained from borings, &c., made by the Barbados Water Supply Company, whose operations were undertaken with a view to supply the rural population of the different parishes with
water up to a height of 750 feet above sea-level. The town of Bridgetown was supplied for many years with an adequate supply of good water by the Bridgetown Water Works Company.

Both companies have been bought up by the Government, and the works are being extended to all the parishes of the Island.

Industry.

The chief articles planted for exportation for some years after the settlement of the island were indigo, cotton-wool, ginger, and aloes; besides several kinds of woods; and the manufacture of sugar does not appear to have been practised with much success till about the middle of the 17th century, when the cultivation of the sugar-cane increased rapidly, and the plant became, in commercial importance, the island's most valuable production. At that period, too, the introduction of African labour was commenced. In 1898 there were 441 sugar-works in operation. The produce of 1871 amounted to 53,800 hogsheads of sugar and 33,500 puncheons of molasses; in 1881, 52,236 hogsheads of sugar, and 33,521 puncheons of molasses. In 1891 the produce amounted to 50,547 hogsheads of sugar and 32,318 puncheons of molasses, as compared with 85,261 hogsheads of sugar, and 51,904 puncheons of molasses in 1890. In 1892, 56,619 hogsheads of sugar, and 43,356 puncheons of molasses. In 1893, 67,157 hogsheads of sugar and 43,374 puncheons of molasses were exported. The exports of produce for the year 1898 amounted to 53,575 hogsheads of sugar, and 34,125 puncheons of molasses. The area under sugar cultivation is estimated at 100,000 acres. In September, 1898, the island, in common with St. Lucia and St. Vincent, suffered severely from the effects of a disastrous hurricane.

Population.

The population of the island in 1851 amounted to 135,939; and although it is estimated that some 20,000 were carried off by cholera in 1854, the census of 1861 showed a total of 152,727 inhabitants. By the census of 1871 there were 162,042 inhabitants, of whom 16,560 were white, and the remainder coloured and black; the natural increase having been checked by the migration to other West Indian Islands of large numbers of the labouring population. In 1881 the total was 171,452; by the census of 1891 the population is returned at 182,306, and is now estimated at 190,000. English is universally spoken. Labour is cheap, and the productive capacity of the soil has been greatly brought out. The island has the appearance of a well-kept garden.

Currency and Banking.

Accounts are kept in sterling, and British coin is legal tender and the chief medium of circulation. There is no limit to the legal tender of British silver, and there is but little gold in circulation. The only bank doing business in Barbados is the Colonial Bank, capital paid up 600,000l. sterling. Total number of branches throughout West Indies 13, with deposits of about 1,500,000l., and a note circulation (five dollar notes) of 350,000l. In Barbados the estimated circulation is 30,000l. There is a Government savings bank which had on 30th September, 1897, 12,716 depositors, and deposits amounting to 218,575l.

Internal Communication.

A railway from Bridgetown to the parish of Saint Andrew (24 miles as surveyed) was commenced in 1889, and completed on 10th September, 1882. The total cost of construction was 195,284l.; the receipts for the year 1897 were 5,503l., exclusive of Government subsidy of 6,000l., and the expenses 5,952l. Of the subsidy of 6,000l. per annum granted by the Legislature, only a sum of 82l. 17s. 6d. was paid in 1897, in consequence of the failure of the Company to comply with the provisions of Act 51 of 1896. It belonged to the Barbados Railway Company, Limited, but was on the 15th July, 1898, purchased by the Foreign American and General Trust Co., Ltd., for the sum of 50,000l. No subsidy was paid during the year 1898. The whole line is under reconstruction.

There is telephonic communication between the police stations by 35 miles of line, which cost 1,465l., and is open to public use. The Barbados Telephone Co. (Limited), a private company contains a total of 470 services, with a total length of line in use of about 600 miles.

Mail Service, Postage, &c.

The Royal Mail steamers arrive in and leave Barbados every alternate week from and to England. There is also fortnightly communication with all the West Indies by these steamers. The usual length of the voyage from England to Barbados is 11 days.

Besides the Royal Mail, a steamer of the West Indian and Pacific, or the Harrison Line, arrives every week from Liverpool.

The direct Scrutton line from London arrives monthly.

The Quebec line of steamers arrive fortnightly from the United States there are also other lines of steamers, viz., the Red Cross Line and Booth Line, which call at Barbados on their voyage from New York to the Brazils and vice versa, at intervals of about 20 days.

The Canadian line of steamers from Halifax arrive monthly. There is a station of the West India and Panama Telegraph Company at Barbados, and direct cable communication with St. Vincent, and thence to the other West Indies, America, and Europe.

Education.

A Government system of elementary education was established by Act No. 41 of the 9th December, 1899.

bor, 1878, which authorised an expenditure not exceeding £15,000 annually. This section of the Act of 1878 has been repealed, and Section 9 (d) of the Education Act Amendment Act, 1897, authorises an annual expenditure of a sum not exceeding £11,000 on elementary education. Grants to higher education made the sum total of expenditure in 1898 £16,360.

The central administration is vested in a Board appointed by the Governor, and the local control conducted by the clergyman of the district assisted by the School Committee. There are 175 schools, with 14,734 scholars (average attendance), and 27,776 on the rolls.

Barbados possesses a college founded by General Codrington, a native of the island, who died in 1710, and whose name it bears. It was affiliated to Durham University in 1875. It is under the administration of the S.P.G., who are the Trustees of General Codrington's will. There are several theological scholarships of the value of £30 per annum from the College funds—though hardly any of these scholarships are at present available owing to lack of funds—and four Island Scholarships at £40 per annum paid from the Colonial Treasury. The latter are confined to natives or sons of natives, or of persons domiciled in the island who have resided therein for at least ten years. There is a good grammar school, called Harrison College, in Bridgetown, established on an old foundation, which has been liberally supported by the Legislature. It has a staff of 7 university men as Masters, a Professor of Chemistry and Agricultural Science, and a Professor of German. The average number of pupils during 1898 was 153. Another First Grade School, "The Lodge," situated in St. John's parish, to the N.E. of the island, was re-opened in 1882, after having been closed for several years. The number of pupils at the close of 1898 was 41. There are four Barbados Scholarships, established by the Education Board, and endowed by the Colony, each of the annual value of £175, tenable at Oxford or Cambridge for four years.

A first grade school for girls was opened in 1888, called the Queen's College. It has a staff of seven mistresses and a music master. The number of pupils was 101 at the close of 1898.

There are four second grade schools for boys, and two for girls. These schools cost the Government, including grants for scholarships, £1,075 annually.

Defence.

Barbados is the headquarters of the military force in the West Indies, having an imperial garrison of 31 officers and 822 non-commissioned officers and men. Charles Fort, on the south west of the island, is a fortified position carrying heavy guns. The Imperial garrison is, however, now in process of transference to St. Lucia. Proposals for the establishment of a volunteer force for local defence are under consideration.

Police, &c.

A police force was established in Barbados in 1835 by an Act of the Legislature, and is stated to have been the first attempt in the British West India Colonies to establish a force of that description upon a similar footing. In 1882 the Harbour Police (established in 1867) were combined with the Land Police. A Juvenile Reformatory was opened in April, 1883.

A lunatic asylum, the construction of which was begun in 1891, supplies a want which had long been felt. A lazaretto is also kept up at the public expense; and there is a general hospital in Bridgetown, to the support of which the colony contributes £6,630 per annum.

Constitution.

The colony possesses representative institutions, but not responsible Government. The Crown has only a veto on legislation, but the Home Government retains the appointment and control of public officers. The Government consists of a Governor, a Legislative Council, consisting of nine members appointed by the Queen, and a House of Assembly, having twenty-four members elected annually on the basis of a moderate franchise. The qualification of members and electors are regulated by a Franchise Act, which became law in April, 1884, and which repeals all previous legislation on the subject. By this Act a liberal extension of the franchise was granted, and about 2,208 electors are registered under its provisions, the number previous to its enactment being only 1,641. This and other Acts relating to the franchise was consolidated by the Representation of the People Act, 1891, which became law on 1st January, 1892, and its amending Act of the 14th July, 1898. The only change made was the extension of the franchise to persons enjoying a pension of £50 a year or more. The number of registered electors for the year 1898 was 1,922. The executive part of the Government consists of the Governor, the Officer commanding the troops, the Colonial Secretary, the Attorney-General or officio, and such other persons as may be nominated by the Queen, one member of the Legislative Council, and four members of the House of Assembly nominated by the Governor. This body is called the Executive Committee, and introduces all money votes, prepares the estimates and initiates all Government measures. The Governor of Barbados was for many years the Governor-in-Chief of the Windward Islands, consisting of Barbados, St. Lucia, St. Vincent, Grenada, and Tobago, but in 1885, by Royal Letters Patent, Barbados was separated from the other Windward Islands, and made a distinct Government.
